readings.purpose: Whether the part was made to size. In-tolerance dimensions remove geometry as the stress concentrator.

title: Why the limit is written down
task: The written limit is well below the critical mass. What is the argument for keeping it there?
scene: Two half-assemblies go on the same bench this afternoon. The procedure sets a mass limit and a spacing, both comfortably inside the calculated physical boundary, and the crew wants to know why the written margin is deliberately larger.
takeaway: Administrative limits create margin against combinations of mass, geometry, reflection, moderation, and ordinary handling error.
why: Criticality depends on mass, geometry, reflection and moderation. Any of those can change by accident. A hand nearby reflects neutrons. A spilled solution moderates them. A second piece on the bench adds mass. The written limit sits far below the physical one, so one human error cannot reach it. It is written down so the margin does not depend on who is on shift. Two of this laboratory's fatal accidents were exactly that error.
assumes: criticality depends on geometry and surroundings as well as on mass
answerText: The written limit is kept well inside the physical boundary so one credible handling mistake or environmental change does not consume the whole margin.

choices: It keeps any single credible handling error from consuming the entire safety margin.
It mainly compensates for uncertainty in the calculated critical mass, so better calculations should let the limit move close to that value.
It guarantees each piece is safe in isolation, so spacing and nearby materials no longer matter once the mass limit is met.
It standardizes inventory control; the surrounding geometry is already fully represented by the critical-mass number.
rebuttals: The written margin is not primarily a penalty for bad theory. It is protection against inputs changing during real handling.
A subcritical piece can still interact with another piece or with reflecting and moderating material nearby.
Critical mass is not a single environment-free number. Geometry and surroundings remain part of the physical problem.

title: High-speed imaging and radiography
task: Estimate the blur distance.
scene: On the analysis table are high-speed photographs from yesterday’s implosion test. Beside them sit several radiographs of the opaque assembly. Each image is labeled with its exposure time. The notebook also lists estimated object speeds and the feature sizes the team wants measured.
takeaway: Exposure time sets a direct spatial-blur limit for rapidly moving objects.
why: Anything moving during the exposure travels a real distance, and that distance becomes motion blur: speed times exposure time. Five hundred metres per second across one microsecond is half a millimetre. That is a resolution limit even if the optics are perfect. Exposure time, viewing angle, penetration, and timing all decide what an image can establish. Blur is especially useful because it is calculable before the shot, so the diagnostic can be designed around the feature size rather than judged afterwards.
assumes: a photograph records everything that happened while the shutter was open

text.setup: An object moves at 500 m/s during a 1 microsecond exposure.

estimate.prompt: An object moving at 500 m/s is recorded with a 1-microsecond (10⁻⁶ s) exposure. Estimate the motion blur in millimetres.
estimate.question: Choose the speed, the exposure time, and the metres-to-millimetres conversion.
estimate.relationship: Motion blur = speed × exposure time. Multiply by 1,000 to turn metres into millimetres.
estimate.explanation: 0.5 mm of blur. Whether that is acceptable is not a property of the camera but a comparison: blur has to be small against the feature being resolved. A boundary moving across a 5 mm gap is measurable at this exposure; a 0.5 mm perturbation is not measurable at all, because it is smeared into its own width. Shortening the exposure is the only lever that does not also cost signal.
givens: Blur distance = speed x exposure time

title: Competing timescales
task: Estimate how far ahead the early side runs, in millimetres.
scene: Several physical clocks run at once during rapid compression, and the design problem lives in the gaps between them. On a test fixture, two initiation channels have different timestamps, and the team has the measured wave speed and a ruler.
takeaway: Processes separated by many orders of magnitude often require different numerical or experimental treatments.
why: Several clocks run at once. Neutron generations multiply on one. The material compresses on another. The assembly begins to blow itself apart on a third. The device works only if multiplication outruns disassembly. These processes differ by many powers of ten, so no single calculation or experiment can hold all of them. The interfaces between them are where it gets hard. This is one: a timing disagreement becomes a geometric error at the speed the wave travels. Half a microsecond is millimetres of asymmetry.
assumes: a wave crosses a distance in a time set by its speed
answerText: About 4 mm.

text.setup: A shock front crosses a test fixture at about 8 x 10^3 m/s. Two initiation channels fire 0.5 microseconds apart.

estimate.prompt: A shock front crosses the assembly at about 8×10³ m/s. Two initiation channels fire 0.5 microseconds (5×10⁻⁷ s) apart. Estimate how far ahead the early side’s front runs by the time the late one starts, in millimetres.
estimate.question: Choose the wave speed, the channel spread, and the metres-to-millimetres conversion.
estimate.relationship: Distance = speed × time. Multiply by 1,000 to turn metres into millimetres.
estimate.explanation: Half a microsecond of disagreement puts one side of the front 4 mm ahead of the other — a visible dent in a convergence that was supposed to be spherical. The timing requirement is written in nanoseconds not because that is what the electronics can manage, but because that is how far the physics moves while the channels argue. Every timing contribution combined later gets judged against this millimetre-scale yardstick.

title: What evidence qualifies a lot?
task: Spend the 100-point test budget on the evidence that can change the release decision for a manufactured lot.
scene: The detonator programme has competing requests and one hundred points of test credit. A production lot is waiting for a release decision, while the bench holds one carefully built prototype, inspection records, and access to a full-system trial.
question: Which measurement tells you whether a production lot is reliable?
takeaway: Reliability is a property of a manufactured population, so acceptance evidence must measure its distribution rather than its best member.
why: A single excellent unit can be repeatable and still say nothing about the next units off the line. Lot acceptance is a population claim. The evidence therefore has to sample the population and measure the spread of the quantity that matters. Dimensional inspection checks conformance to a drawing, not timing performance. A full-system test mixes too many causes together. Sampling several lots gives a distribution, exposes tails, and directly answers the decision the programme must make.
assumes: a sample can estimate the spread of a production population
a component test is more diagnostic than an integrated test when the component itself is the question
answerText: Spend the test budget sampling several lots and measuring the timing spread of each. That evidence directly tests the population being accepted.

choices: Sample several lots and measure the timing spread of each.
Build one unit to the best achievable standard and fire it repeatedly.
Tighten the drawing tolerances and re-inspect the parts dimensionally.
Wait for the first full-system trial and judge the detonators from it.
rebuttals: One unit fired repeatedly measures that unit. It says nothing about the next thirty off the line, which is what the device will be built from.
Dimensional inspection catches parts outside the drawing. The requirement here is written in nanoseconds, and two parts inside the same tolerance can fire measurably apart.
Waiting for the full-system trial makes every component a suspect at once when it disappoints, and there is one trial.
text.setup: The detonator program has three competing requests for its next 100 credits.

why_this_format: The stop is explicitly a scarce-budget evidence decision. VALUE makes every attractive test consume the whole budget and grades whether the purchased evidence can actually change a lot-release decision.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Four 100-credit options compete for a 100-credit budget, so the board costs 400 credits. Only the multi-lot timing sample is decisive for the release decision, and the options span population timing, single-unit repeatability, dimensional conformance, and integrated-system outcome.

data.hint: You can buy one test plan. Read what each plan would reveal before spending the credits; the release decision is about the manufactured population.
data.decision: Release or hold a production lot based on evidence about its timing-performance distribution.

options.label: Sample several lots and measure timing spread
options.reveals: Whether the manufactured population, including its tail, meets the timing-performance requirement.

options.label: Build one best-achievable unit and fire it repeatedly
options.reveals: How repeatable one specially prepared unit is, without showing lot-to-lot or unit-to-unit spread.

options.label: Tighten drawing tolerances and re-inspect dimensions
options.reveals: Whether parts match the drawing more closely, not whether accepted parts fire with the required timing spread.

options.label: Wait for the next full-system trial
options.reveals: Whether the whole system performed, while leaving many component causes entangled if it did not.

failure_feedback.consequence: the programme learns a great deal about one unit and almost nothing about the lot it must accept
failure_feedback.line: You qualified a specimen, not a population.

failure_feedback.consequence: a bad result leaves many components as suspects and a good result still does not measure the lot tail
failure_feedback.line: Integration is not a substitute for component acceptance data.

title: Synchronizing many channels
task: Estimate sigma_total.
scene: The timing-budget meeting has stalled. Each subsystem lead insists that their contribution is small, yet the combined requirement is close enough that nobody wants to sign it. The system cannot move to the next review until one number closes the argument.
takeaway: A timing budget must include the full measurement chain.
why: The physical system contributes some delay, cable lengths contribute more, a trigger threshold shifts the moment a pulse is registered, and the recording instrument adds its own. Los Alamos handles this by building a timing budget: every contribution named, measured and combined. Independent contributions add in quadrature — squared, summed, square-rooted — so the largest term dominates and several smaller ones still raise the total. Two, three and four nanoseconds do not make nine; they make about five and a half.
assumes: independent errors do not simply add
answerText: sigma_total = sqrt(29), about 5.4 ns.

text.setup: Three independent timing contributions are a 2 ns shared trigger, 3 ns of cable delay, and 4 ns of diagnostic registration.

estimate.prompt: Three independent timing contributions — a shared trigger at 2 ns, cable delay at 3 ns, and diagnostic registration at 4 ns — must be combined. Estimate the total timing uncertainty.
estimate.question: Choose the three component uncertainties to combine in quadrature.
estimate.relationship: Independent timing errors add in quadrature: the root of the sum of the squares. They do not add straight.
estimate.explanation: Quadrature gives 5.4 ns, well under the 9 ns a straight sum predicts, because independent errors do not all peak together — and the 4 ns recorder term alone carries more than half the total variance, so it is the one worth attacking first. Then check the answer against what the front does with that time: at 8×10³ m/s, 5.4 ns is about 0.04 mm of lead. Comfortably inside a millimetre-scale symmetry limit, which a half-microsecond spread would not be.
givens: Do not add signs, because these are uncertainty scales

title: Carrying uncertainty through
task: Estimate the total fractional uncertainty.
scene: A predicted reaction rate rests on a cross section known to a few per cent and a flux known to a few more. Theory is being asked how well the prediction is known.
takeaway: Adding independent uncertainties linearly is usually too pessimistic; ignoring correlation can be too optimistic.
why: Independent uncertainties combine in quadrature: square each contribution, add the squares, and take the root. Eight percent and six percent make ten, not fourteen. The larger term dominates, so reducing a small contribution may barely change the total while improving the largest one matters much more. That ranking is the practical value of an uncertainty budget. It tells a laboratory with limited people and time which measurement is worth improving first, rather than treating every error bar as equally urgent.
assumes: two independent errors are unlikely to be wrong the same way at once
answerText: About 10%.

text.setup: A predicted reaction rate has an 8% cross-section uncertainty and a 6% flux uncertainty.

estimate.prompt: A predicted reaction rate carries an 8% cross-section uncertainty and a 6% flux uncertainty, and the two are independent. Estimate the combined uncertainty.
estimate.question: Choose the two component uncertainties to combine in quadrature.
estimate.relationship: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature: the root of the sum of the squares.
estimate.explanation: Quadrature gives 10%, not the 14% of a straight sum: independent errors partly cancel. Note also that the larger component dominates — halving the 6% would move the total to about 8.5%, while halving the 8% would move it to 7.2%.
givens: Independent fractional uncertainties combine in quadrature

title: Where the fragments go
task: A nucleus at rest splits into a heavy and a light fragment. Which carries more kinetic energy?
scene: A nucleus initially at rest splits into a heavy fragment and a light fragment. The team has measured the fragment masses and is arguing about which one should carry the larger share of kinetic energy before looking at the detector data.
takeaway: Momentum conservation fixes the ratio of fragment speeds, and energy follows from it.
why: The nucleus starts at rest, so total momentum is zero. The two fragments therefore leave with equal and opposite momentum. The lighter fragment must move faster because the momentum magnitude is the same for both. Kinetic energy can be written as p²/(2m). At equal momentum, the smaller mass has the larger kinetic energy. Momentum conservation fixes the relation between the motions; the energy formula then tells how the released energy is divided.
assumes: momentum is conserved in an isolated system
answerText: The lighter fragment carries more kinetic energy. Equal and opposite momenta imply K = p²/(2m), so at the same |p| the smaller mass has the larger kinetic energy.

choices: The lighter one: equal and opposite momenta give it the greater speed.
The heavier one: kinetic energy rises with the mass of the fragment.
They share it equally, since momentum is conserved in the split.
It cannot be decided without knowing the two binding energies.
rebuttals: Kinetic energy at fixed momentum falls with mass rather than rising with it.
Equal momenta do not mean equal energies, because energy depends on momentum squared over mass.
The binding energies fix the total energy released, not how it divides between the fragments.
text.call: Recognize measurements that share an error

title: Build the implosion uncertainty budget
task: Read the whole reading panel, then select the two causes that together account for every reading. No single cause does.
scene: An implosion trial has returned two anomalies, and the next development cycle can afford only one major push. Division leads are waiting outside the analysis room to learn where the effort goes. Name the wrong source and weeks disappear into the wrong fix.
takeaway: Improvement starts by naming the dominant source of uncertainty.
why: A budget lists the separate contributions: material properties, geometry, timing, diagnostics, models. For each one it estimates how much it moves the final claim. Its value is not the total but the ranking. Improvement starts with the dominant source, and effort spent anywhere else changes nothing. The honesty of it matters here too. When two anomalies sit in different subsystems, the budget has two entries. Force one cause onto both and you misattribute one of them — and that is the entry somebody then goes and works on.
assumes: two problems can have two different causes
answerText: Explosive lot-to-lot wave-speed variation + Attenuation-model error in the density inversion

text.setup: You are assigning an implosion trial's anomalies to the right uncertainty terms.

panel.title: Two entries in one budget
panel.hook: A trial has come back with two problems: the initiation channels arrived over a wider spread than budgeted, and the inferred peak density is below prediction. The budget has to name causes, and no single entry accounts for both.
panel.riddle: Select the two causes that together account for every reading. No single cause does.

readings.name: Channel arrival spread
readings.purpose: How closely the initiation channels agreed. A wide spread has several possible sources in hardware and in the explosive itself.

readings.name: Explosive lot wave-speed certificates
readings.observed: spread of 2.4% across the lots used
readings.reference: within 0.5% for a single qualified lot
readings.purpose: Whether the segments came from material with consistent detonation velocity. Lot-to-lot spread converts directly into arrival-time spread.

readings.name: Segment placement metrology
readings.purpose: Where the segments actually sat. Placement error changes path lengths and therefore arrival times.

readings.name: Shared trigger self-test
readings.purpose: Whether the common trigger fired when commanded. A trigger fault moves channels without any material or geometric cause.

readings.name: Inferred peak density
readings.purpose: The end product of the analysis chain. It depends on the radiographic data and on the model used to convert that data into density.

readings.name: Raw radiographic transmission
readings.purpose: The measurement before interpretation. Normal raw data with an abnormal inferred result points at the conversion rather than the observation.

readings.name: Attenuation calibration against a step wedge
readings.purpose: Whether the model that turns transmission into density is correct where it is being used. A calibration that fails at high density biases exactly the result being reported.

title: Acceptance criteria
task: Estimate the conservative lower bound of the measurement.
scene: A property has to be at least a hundred units and the measurement reads a hundred and two, plus or minus three. Material this scarce cannot be scrapped casually, or accepted on hope.
takeaway: Acceptance criteria need explicit rules for uncertainty and borderline results.
why: An acceptance criterion turns a desired property into a rule: a limit, a measurement method, and a stated uncertainty. Results near the boundary are why the uncertainty rule must be agreed before the number is known. Here the central value is 102, but the lower plausible value is 99. That falls below the 100-unit requirement, so the measurement does not demonstrate a clean pass. Reading only the midpoint treats an uncertain measurement as though it were exact.
assumes: a measurement has a range, not just a value
answerText: About 99 units, which is below the 100-unit threshold, so it is not an unambiguous pass.

text.setup: A property must be at least 100 units. The measurement is 102 with uncertainty +/-3 units.

estimate.prompt: A property must be at least 100 units. The measurement reads 102 units with an uncertainty of ±3 units. Estimate the conservative lower bound.
estimate.question: Choose the measured value and the uncertainty.
estimate.relationship: The lower bound of a result = the measured value − its uncertainty. Compare that against the threshold, not the central value.
estimate.explanation: The lower bound of 99 falls below the 100-unit threshold, so a measurement that reads above the limit still does not demonstrate compliance. The margin has to exceed the uncertainty before a pass is unambiguous.
estimate.solution: 102 − 3 ≈ 99 units, which falls below a 100-unit threshold.
givens: The lower plausible value is about 99

title: Buy the test that can decide
task: Spend the single week of facility time on the test whose possible outcomes would separate the competing timing hypotheses.
scene: Three team leads are waiting outside the facility office, each with a test they say cannot wait. There is one week of access left in the schedule, and only one proposal can take it. The scheduler needs one name before Monday.
question: Which test changes the programme's next decision?
takeaway: A test is valuable when its possible outcomes distinguish competing explanations, not when it merely produces more data.
why: Before a test is run, each hypothesis should predict what the chosen observable will do. If both hypotheses predict the same trace, even perfect data cannot separate them. Repeating one condition can reduce statistical uncertainty while leaving the decision unchanged. A large integrated shot can also be ambiguous if several causes move the same output. The valuable test is the smallest one whose outcomes differ between the hypotheses, with diagnostics aimed directly at that difference.
assumes: an experiment is useful when different explanations predict different outcomes
facility time is limited
answerText: Use the week on the small test that cleanly separates the two timing hypotheses. Its outcomes point to different explanations, so the result changes what the programme does next.

choices: A small test that cleanly separates the two competing timing hypotheses.
A full-scale assembly shot, with the diagnostics that will fit around it.
A long series of repeat shots at one condition, for the statistics.
A repeat of last month’s test, whose configuration record was never written up.
rebuttals: A full assembly with limited diagnostics produces a spectacular record with too many possible causes to attribute anything to.
Repeating one condition measures the scatter at a point already known, and separates no hypothesis at all.
A repeat with no configuration record cannot be compared with the shot it is repeating, which is the only thing that would have made it useful.
text.setup: Three test concepts compete for one week of facility time.

why_this_format: The current multiple choice describes value-of-information reasoning but does not make the cost visible. VALUE forces the player to spend the only facility week and inspect what each option would actually reveal.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Each of four plans costs one week while the budget is one week, so the board costs four times the budget. Only the discriminating timing test is decisive, and the options cover hypothesis separation, integrated performance, repeatability, and comparability/provenance.

data.hint: You have one facility week. Open each plan to see what its result would tell you, then spend the week on the evidence that can separate the two timing explanations.
data.decision: Choose which timing explanation to pursue in the next design cycle.

options.label: Small test aimed at the timing signature where the hypotheses differ
options.reveals: Which timing hypothesis survives when the one observable they predict differently is measured.

options.label: Full-scale assembly shot with limited diagnostics
options.reveals: Whether the integrated assembly performs well or badly, while leaving several causes capable of producing the same result.

options.label: Long repeat series at the already-tested condition
options.reveals: The statistical scatter at a condition already known, without distinguishing the two explanations.

options.label: Repeat last month's poorly documented configuration
options.reveals: A new outcome that cannot be cleanly compared with the old one because the original configuration is uncertain.

failure_feedback.consequence: the outcome is impressive but several hypotheses can still explain it
failure_feedback.line: A bigger test is not a more discriminating test.

failure_feedback.action: buying more repeats of the same condition
failure_feedback.consequence: the error bar shrinks around a measurement that both hypotheses already predict
failure_feedback.line: Precision did not buy a decision.

title: Critical path to an integrated trial
task: Estimate how much a parallel chain can slip before it controls the date.
scene: Three chains of work are running in parallel, and the integrated trial cannot happen until the longest one finishes. Fat Man's schedule is managed this way: the calendar is controlled by dependencies, not by how many tasks look busy.
takeaway: Schedule management starts with dependencies, not activity counts.
why: The longest chain is the critical path. It is the only place where adding people or shifts moves the date. Effort poured into a task that is not on it changes nothing, however busy it makes everyone. It is spent on float that was already there. Float is the gap between the controlling chain and the one being worked on, and it is finite. Enough slippage on a parallel chain makes that chain the new critical path. At which point the whole calculation has to be done again.
assumes: work that can happen in parallel does not add up
answerText: Two weeks of float; a third week of slippage makes it the new critical path.

text.setup: A simplified schedule has three dependency chains: lens inspection at 3 + 4 + 2 weeks, electrical qualification at 2 + 3 + 2, and casing work at 2 + 2 + 3.

estimate.prompt: The controlling chain of an integrated trial runs 9 weeks. A parallel chain in the same trial runs 7 weeks. Estimate how much the parallel chain can slip before it becomes the chain that sets the date.
estimate.question: Choose the controlling chain duration and the parallel chain duration.
estimate.relationship: Float on a parallel chain = the length of the controlling chain − the length of that chain.
estimate.explanation: The parallel chain carries two weeks of slack: two weeks of trouble there costs the programme nothing, and a third week makes it the new critical path. This is why adding people to work off the critical path buys no schedule at all — the effort is spent on float that already existed. Manage the float, not just the length.
givens: Lens inspection chain totals 9 weeks and controls the date

title: What a scaled shot can and cannot tell you
task: A half-scale shot is fired. Which of its results transfer to full scale?
scene: A half-scale shot is proposed: an eighth of the explosive and a much shorter schedule. The material detonation velocity is listed at both scales, and the team has geometric dimensions, reaction-zone measurements, and timing records spread across the table.
takeaway: A scaled experiment reproduces the dimensionless quantities, and only what depends on them transfers.
why: Scaling works through dimensionless groups: reproduce those and the phenomena they govern reproduce too. What does not scale is anything with a dimension of its own — a detonation velocity, a diffusion length, a reaction time — because halving the geometry does not halve them. So a half-scale shot can settle a symmetry question governed by ratios and cannot settle a timing margin measured in microseconds. The discipline is to state, before firing, which quantities the shot is entitled to decide.
assumes: a dimensionless ratio has the same value at any scale
answerText: Only conclusions governed by matched dimensionless groups transfer directly. Effects tied to fixed material length or time scales must be checked separately.

choices: Transfer only conclusions governed by matched dimensionless ratios; re-check effects tied to fixed material length or time scales.
Transfer the wave timing directly because detonation velocity is unchanged, even though every geometric path is shorter.
Transfer all geometric and timing conclusions after multiplying lengths and times by the same scale factor.
Treat the scaled shot as qualitative only, because material properties prevent any quantitative similarity between scales.
rebuttals: Unchanged velocity does not make absolute timing transferable when the path length changes.
A single scale factor works only when every relevant physical length and time scales with the geometry; intrinsic material scales do not.
Scaled experiments can be quantitatively predictive when the dimensionless groups governing the phenomenon are matched.

title: What Trinity had to answer
task: Match each question Trinity must answer to the evidence that can actually settle that question.
scene: Trinity is being written as a set of questions before it becomes an event. One full-system attempt will carry dozens of expectations, and every division wants its own result treated as decisive. There will be no second shot to clarify what the first one meant.
takeaway: A full-system test should be written as a set of questions before it becomes an event.
why: A test without its questions written down in advance becomes an argument afterwards about what it proved. Different questions need different evidence. Full-system nuclear performance requires the integrated event. Firing-system coordination comes from timing records and can be judged even if another part disappoints. Comparing observed effects with pre-test predictions tests the model. Safety evidence addresses hazards at and beyond the site. Writing those questions first keeps one dramatic outcome from swallowing every other claim the experiment was designed to answer.
assumes: a test proves what it was designed to ask
answerText: Integrated nuclear performance -> Full-system yield/effects record; firing coordination -> Independent timing traces; model validation -> Comparison with the pre-test prediction envelope; hazards -> Post-event measurements that track exposure, contamination, and changing conditions for people and surroundings.

choices: The full-system yield and effects record from the event itself.
Independent timing traces showing when the firing and diagnostic channels acted.
A comparison between observed effects and the prediction envelope written before the shot.
A set of measurements collected after the event that tracks exposure, contamination, and changing conditions for people and surroundings.
rebuttals: Only the integrated event can answer the full-system performance question; component timing traces cannot substitute for it.
Coordination is a timing question, so it needs time-resolved records rather than a single overall outcome.
Model validation requires a prediction made before the observation, then a direct comparison with what occurred.
Consequences affecting people and surroundings cannot be read from the overall event alone. They need observations that continue afterward and show what changed where.
scenarios: Would the integrated implosion configuration produce the predicted nuclear chain reaction?
Did the firing and initiation system act in the required coordinated sequence?
How did observed effects compare with the broad range of pre-test yield predictions?
What radiological and physical hazards existed at and beyond the site?
text.setup: Match each pre-shot question to the evidence that can settle it.

title: Trinity field engineering
task: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
scene: The desert crew has the tower, cables, cameras, power, and communications spread across a schedule that is running out of room. The weather window will not wait for a missed interface. Every team wants to know whether the field is truly ready.
takeaway: Field integration is ordered so that every interface is proved before the thing that needs it arrives.
why: Field integration succeeds or fails on interfaces, and each interface has to be proved before the thing that depends on it arrives. Site survey, power, communications, and controlled access come first. Electrical and diagnostic interfaces are installed and independently inspected while replacement is still possible. Only then does the approved assembly enter the field configuration. The countdown runs against defined hold points, and the site is secured and documented afterwards. The order preserves the ability to find and correct a failed interface before it becomes buried inside the next step.
assumes: a schedule set by weather cannot be extended
answerText: 1. Survey the site and establish power, communications and controlled access, which everything after this runs on. 2. Install and independently inspect each electrical and diagnostic interface, while there is still time to replace one. 3. Bring the approved assembly into the field configuration, once every interface it will use has been proved. 4. Run the countdown against defined hold points, then secure and document the site.

rebuttals: Survey, power, communications and access come first. Everything after this runs on them, and none of it can be installed before they exist.
Install and independently inspect each interface second — while there is still time to replace one, which is the whole reason it is here rather than later.
Bring the assembly into field configuration third, after every interface it will use has been proved. Once it is at the tower, fixing a cable means undoing this step.
Run the countdown against hold points and document the site last. A hold point is what makes a countdown stoppable rather than a commitment.
cards: Survey the site and establish power, communications and controlled access.
Install each electrical and diagnostic interface, and have every one independently inspected.
Bring the approved assembly up the tower into its field configuration.
Run the countdown against the defined hold points, and record what every instrument saw.
text.setup: Order the field-integration sequence.

title: The plot that makes a decay a straight line
task: Which transformation makes exponential decay linear, and what physical quantity comes from the slope?
scene: Two counters have produced a table of count rate against time, and the notebook has it plotted on ordinary axes as a curve that nobody can read a number off.
takeaway: Plotting a logarithm turns an exponential into a straight line, and its slope is the decay constant.
why: An exponential plotted on linear axes is a curve, which is hard to check by eye. Take the logarithm of the count rate and the same data becomes a straight line. Its slope is minus the decay constant, so the half-life follows from t½ = ln2/λ. The transformed plot also exposes failures: a second component can change the slope, while background can flatten the line at late times. Choosing the axes is part of the measurement.
assumes: a logarithm turns a constant ratio into a constant difference
answerText: Plot ln(count rate) versus time. The slope is −λ, and the half-life follows from t½ = ln2/λ.

choices: Plot ln(count rate) against time; the slope is −λ, so t½ = ln2/λ.
Plot count rate against time and fit a straight line to the late-time points; the slope is −λ.
Plot ln(count rate) against ln(time); the slope is −λ for any radioactive decay.
Plot 1/(count rate) against time; the slope gives the half-life directly.
rebuttals: A straight-line fit on linear axes is only a local approximation to an exponential and its slope changes with time.
A log-log plot linearizes power laws. Exponential decay becomes linear when only the count-rate axis is logged.
Taking the reciprocal does not turn an exponential into a line; it produces another exponential.

title: Where the energy in fission comes from
task: Why does splitting uranium release energy while splitting carbon would absorb it?
scene: A visitor asks why splitting a heavy nucleus releases energy while splitting a light one costs energy. The blackboard has the binding-energy curve on it and nobody has used it to answer.
takeaway: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve says which way a nuclear reaction releases energy.
why: Binding energy per nucleon rises steeply from hydrogen, peaks around iron and nickel, and falls slowly to uranium. A reaction releases energy when its products sit HIGHER on that curve than its reactants, because the products are more tightly bound. Uranium splitting into two mid-mass fragments moves up the curve, so energy comes out. Carbon splitting would move down it, so energy would have to go in. The same curve is why fusion of light nuclei also releases energy — from the other side of the peak.
assumes: a nucleus is held together by binding energy
answerText: Fission releases energy when the products are more tightly bound per nucleon than the original heavy nucleus. The mass difference between those states appears as released energy.

choices: The fragments lie higher on the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, so the products are more tightly bound and the mass difference appears as released energy.
The fragments separate electrically after the split, so nearly all released energy is simply Coulomb repulsion and the binding-energy change is secondary bookkeeping.
Any heavy nucleus releases energy when divided because the same mass is distributed among more particles and therefore more kinetic degrees of freedom.
Uranium releases energy because it is radioactive; a stable nucleus such as carbon would have no available nuclear energy to release.
rebuttals: Coulomb repulsion contributes to why heavy nuclei are less tightly bound, but the reaction energy is the total binding-energy difference between initial and final nuclei.
The number of fragments does not determine the sign of the reaction energy. The binding energies of reactants and products do.
Radioactivity concerns whether a process occurs spontaneously and how fast. The energy balance is set by the masses and binding energies of the states.

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Compare a prediction band with an observation
task: Estimate the offset in units of the measurement uncertainty, then state the strongest justified conclusion.
scene: A model predicts an observable between fifteen and twenty-five units. The measurement reads twenty-one, plus or minus two. The temptation after Trinity is to read one comparison as a verdict on everything.
takeaway: Evidence should update a model claim by claim, not by declaring total victory.
why: The gap between an observation and a prediction is measured in units of the measurement's own uncertainty. Take the difference and divide by that uncertainty. Half a sigma from the middle of the band is consistent. But consistency with a band this wide is weak evidence, because fifteen to twenty-five would have accommodated almost anything. Agreement supports the part of the model that produced the band, and no more. One agreeing diagnostic can sit beside others that disagree, and those still need explaining.
assumes: a wide prediction is easy to agree with
answerText: |21 - 20|/2 = 0.5 sigma. The observation is consistent with the prediction band, but a band that wide makes consistency weak evidence; it does not confirm every model assumption, and diagnostics that disagree with each other still need explaining.

text.setup: A classroom model predicts an observable between 15 and 25 units; the measurement reads 21 units with an uncertainty of +/-2.

estimate.prompt: A model predicts an observable between 15 and 25 units, so its midpoint is 20. The measurement reads 21 units with an uncertainty of ±2. Estimate the offset in units of the measurement uncertainty.
estimate.question: Choose the observed value, the band midpoint, and the measurement uncertainty.
estimate.relationship: Distance in sigma = |observed − predicted| ÷ the measurement uncertainty.
estimate.explanation: Half a sigma is no disagreement at all — at this precision the observation and the midpoint are indistinguishable. Be careful what that licenses: it says the measurement is consistent with the model, not that the model is confirmed. A band 10 units wide is easy to agree with, so consistency here is weak evidence, and diagnostics that disagree with each other still need explaining.

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Why separation is a physical problem
task: Why is ordinary chemistry a poor way to separate uranium-235 from uranium-238 in bulk?
scene: At Chemistry and Metallurgy, a production planner brings a request to enrich uranium-235 relative to uranium-238 by an ordinary chemical route. The division has been asked to decide whether the two isotopes give chemistry enough contrast to make that plan practical.
takeaway: Isotopes of one element have nearly the same electron structure, so practical enrichment must exploit a tiny isotope-dependent physical difference.
why: Chemical behaviour is controlled mainly by electrons, and the two uranium isotopes have the same electron count and almost the same electronic structure. Their ordinary chemical reactions are therefore nearly identical. The useful contrast is the small mass difference, about one part in 235, which can be exploited by processes that respond to mass or mass-to-charge ratio. The tiny size of that contrast is why isotope enrichment requires repeated separation stages rather than one ordinary chemical reaction.
assumes: chemical behaviour is set by electrons, and isotopes differ only in the nucleus
answerText: Ordinary chemistry offers almost no selectivity because the isotopes have nearly identical electron structures. Enrichment has to exploit a small isotope-dependent physical difference, especially mass.

choices: Their electron structures are nearly identical, so ordinary chemical reactions provide almost no selectivity; enrichment instead exploits a small isotope-dependent physical difference.
Their chemical reaction rates differ enough for separation, but the difference is too slow to be useful only because uranium compounds are difficult to handle.
Their densities differ by about one part in 235, so settling or filtration is the natural route but requires extremely long columns.
Their radioactivities differ, so radiation detectors can sort individual atoms even though the chemistry itself cannot.
rebuttals: The limitation is not mainly reaction speed or handling. The electronic structures that drive ordinary chemistry are almost the same.
A tiny isotope mass difference does not make bulk solutions separate by ordinary settling or filtration.
A detector can identify radiation from a population, but that does not provide a practical chemical force that sorts neutral atoms into separate bulk streams.

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Spend the follow-up checks on independence
task: Choose two follow-up checks. Buy evidence that can distinguish a shared calibration problem from a real physics discrepancy.
scene: Theory and experiment disagree by three standard deviations. The division can complete two follow-up checks before the next review, and every extra run that repeats the same dependency consumes one of those chances.
question: Which two checks can change the interpretation of the disagreement?
takeaway: When theory and experiment disagree, the next measurements should attack shared systematics and add evidence based on different dependencies.
why: More of the same data reduces random error but carries the same systematic dependencies. Retuning the model can hide the discrepancy without explaining it. First audit the calibration shared by the measurements, because a common bias can create a confident disagreement. Then use a measurement based on different hardware or a different calibration path. If the discrepancy survives independent evidence, the case for missing physics strengthens. If it disappears, the original measurement chain becomes the leading suspect.
assumes: a systematic error does not average away with more repeats
independent measurements should not share the same critical calibration
answerText: Use the two checks on the shared-calibration audit and an independent measurement with a different dependency chain. Together they can distinguish common bias from a discrepancy that survives independent evidence.

choices: Audit the shared calibrations, then design a measurement that tells the explanations apart.
Retune the uncertain parameters until the model reproduces the measurement.
Collect more of the same data, to see whether the gap narrows.
Adopt the experimental value and record the disagreement in the report.
rebuttals: Retuning parameters to force agreement hides the discrepancy inside a number and destroys the only evidence that something was wrong.
More of the same data carries the same systematic. It narrows the statistical error around a value that may be biased.
Adopting the experimental value settles the disagreement by whoever wrote it down last, and leaves the cause in place for the next comparison.
text.setup: Theory and experiment disagree by three standard deviations.

why_this_format: The original correct option contains two distinct evidence moves. VALUE turns them into a limited budget: the player must spend on independence instead of buying more precision from the same chain.
trap_is_satisfied_by: invented decision budget of two follow-up checks: four one-check options cost four in total, only the shared-calibration audit and the independent measurement are decisive, and they probe two distinct evidence axes.

data.hint: You can fund two checks. Read what each one would reveal. One should test a shared dependency; the other should stand on a different measurement chain.
data.decision: Decide whether the three-sigma gap is best treated as a shared systematic or as a discrepancy that survives independent measurement.

options.reveals: Whether a common calibration bias can account for the apparent disagreement.

options.label: Repeat the observable with a different detector or calibration path
options.reveals: Whether the discrepancy survives when the critical dependency chain changes.

options.label: Collect more data with the same setup
options.reveals: A smaller random error bar around a result that still carries the same systematic dependencies.

options.label: Retune uncertain model parameters until the curves agree
options.reveals: That the model can be adjusted to match the datum, without identifying why the original prediction missed it.

failure_feedback.action: spending both checks on more of the same data
failure_feedback.consequence: the statistical error shrinks while a shared calibration bias remains untouched
failure_feedback.line: You made the disagreement more precise, not more independent.

failure_feedback.consequence: the discrepancy is absorbed into model parameters and the evidence about its cause is lost
failure_feedback.line: A fit can hide a problem without locating it.

dayTitle: Reconcile evidence and freeze the design
title: Post-Trinity design freeze
task: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
scene: Trinity has produced new evidence, and a last-minute improvement is already being argued over. Drawings are moving toward production while engineers are still proposing changes. The room has one uncomfortable question: what can still change without severing the link to what was tested?
takeaway: A freeze comes before the paperwork, or the paperwork describes something still changing.
why: Each stage is the input to the next. The timing, hydrodynamic and radiation records are reconciled into one account of the shot, because there is nothing to compare until they agree with each other. That account is then compared with the pre-test predictions, and what remains unexplained is named rather than absorbed. Only then can the evidence-supported changes be approved and the configuration frozen. The freeze comes before the paperwork — reverse those two and the documents describe a configuration that is still moving.
assumes: what was tested and what gets built can drift apart
answerText: 1. Recover and reconcile the timing, hydrodynamic and radiation records into one account of the shot. 2. Compare that account with the pre-test predictions, and name what is still unexplained. 3. Approve only the changes the evidence supports, and freeze the configuration. 4. Update assembly records, procedures and training against the frozen configuration.

rebuttals: Reconcile the records into one account of the shot first. Three disagreeing records are not evidence about anything yet.
Compare that account with the pre-test predictions second, and name what is still unexplained. An unnamed discrepancy is one nobody will return to.
Approve only the evidence-supported changes and freeze the configuration third. This is the step that ties the article to the test.
Update records, procedures and training last, against the frozen configuration. Do it earlier and the paperwork describes something still changing.

Compare that account with the pre-test predictions, and name what is still unexplained.
Approve only the changes the evidence supports, and freeze the configuration.
Update assembly records, procedures and training against the frozen configuration.

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Why light nuclei release energy too
task: If fusion releases energy, why is it difficult to start?
scene: The binding-energy curve on the board rises steeply from light nuclei toward iron. A younger theorist has noticed that fusion moves uphill on that same curve and asks why an energy-releasing reaction does not simply happen whenever light nuclei meet.
takeaway: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy for the same reason fission of heavy ones does, and it is harder to start.
why: Fusion moves up the binding-energy curve from the light end, so it releases energy — more per nucleon than fission does. The difficulty is getting there: two positive nuclei repel, and the nuclear force that binds them only reaches across about a femtometre. Closing that gap needs kinetic energy, which means temperatures of millions of kelvin, whereas fission needs only a slow neutron and no barrier at all. Energy released and ease of ignition are separate questions, and confusing them is the usual error.
assumes: like charges repel, and the nuclear force acts only at very short range
answerText: Fusion can release energy and still be hard to start because two positive nuclei repel each other. They must get extremely close before the short-range nuclear force can bind them.

choices: The nuclei are positively charged, so they must approach through electrostatic repulsion before the short-range nuclear force can bind them.
The products are more tightly bound, but the released energy cannot appear until a neutron first removes the electrical charge barrier.
The strong nuclear force becomes effective only when nuclei are moving rapidly, so high temperature is needed to strengthen the force itself.
Light nuclei are already close to the peak of the binding-energy curve, so fusion releases too little energy to sustain further reactions.
rebuttals: A neutron is not required to remove the Coulomb barrier in ordinary light-nucleus fusion; the reactant nuclei themselves must get close enough to interact.
The nuclear force is short-ranged, not switched on by high speed. High kinetic energy helps the nuclei approach despite their electrostatic repulsion.
Light nuclei begin well below the iron peak in binding energy per nucleon, which is why fusion can release substantial energy.

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Final diagnostic readiness review
task: Arrange the four cards from earliest cause or prerequisite to latest result.
scene: The final readiness review asks whether the instruments will actually record what happens. There is exactly one event to record, no repeat shot to recover a missed observable, and a diagnostic that saturates or loses timing can erase an answer permanently.
takeaway: The final product is a trustworthy evidence system, not merely a collection of sensors.
why: Calibration and configuration records come first. An instrument nobody can describe afterwards produces data nobody can use. End-to-end timing and health checks then prove the chain works as a chain, rather than as a set of working parts. Independent coverage of the critical observables comes next — independent, so one failure does not take a whole answer with it. Deployment is approved with the residual risks named and a backup for each. Readiness means failures will be recognised, not that there are none.
assumes: an instrument can be working and still miss the event
answerText: 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 (Verify calibration and configuration records -> Run end-to-end timing and health checks -> Demonstrate independent coverage of critical observables -> Approve deployment with named residual risks and contingencies)

rebuttals: Verify calibration and configuration records first. An instrument nobody can describe afterwards produces data nobody can use.
Run end-to-end timing and health checks second. Every part working is not the same as the chain working.
Demonstrate independent coverage of the critical observables third, so one failure does not take a whole answer with it.
Approve deployment with named residual risks and contingencies last. Readiness means failures will be recognised, not that there are none.

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Leave a materials capability, not just better numbers
task: Spend the final 100-credit improvement budget on the evidence system that will remain useful when the next batch behaves differently.
scene: The final dossier has to show more than that components existed. The division has one last hundred credits of improvement to spend, and the choice says what it thinks a materials capability is.
question: Which investment creates the most durable materials capability?
takeaway: A durable materials programme links process conditions to composition, structure, properties, and traceable batch records.
why: Another measurement can describe one batch more precisely, but it does not explain why the next batch differs. A process-to-properties record connects what was done to what the material became. That relationship can be tested across batches and used later to diagnose a change in structure or performance. Extra composition checks, tighter remeasurement, and higher throughput all have value, but none creates that causal record. The durable capability is the evidence chain linking process history to measured properties.
assumes: future batches may differ from today's batch
a record is useful when it preserves relationships, not only isolated measurements
answerText: Spend the 100 credits on records that link each batch's process conditions to its measured composition, structure, and properties. That creates an evidence chain future staff can use to explain variation.

choices: Records linking each batch’s conditions to its measured properties.
Independent composition measurements and microscope work on every batch.
Re-measurement of the batches already released, to a tighter tolerance.
Higher production throughput, with the measurements and records unchanged.
rebuttals: Independent composition measurements and microscope work verify a batch and are already required. They produce more measurements with nothing connecting them.
Re-measuring released material improves numbers on parts that are already installed and links none of them to how they were made.
More throughput on the same records makes more material that nobody can characterise afterwards.
text.setup: The division has one final 100-credit improvement budget.

why_this_format: The stop already presents a final fixed improvement budget. VALUE makes the player inspect what each investment would reveal in the future rather than choosing the most virtuous-sounding sentence.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Four 100-credit investments compete for a 100-credit budget, so the board costs 400 credits. The process-to-properties record is decisive for diagnosing future batch variation, and the options span traceability, verification, precision, and throughput.

data.hint: You can fund one improvement. Open each option and ask what a future team would learn when a later batch comes out different.
data.decision: Choose the improvement that best preserves the ability to explain and correct future batch variation.

options.label: Link each batch's process conditions to measured properties
options.reveals: Which process conditions consistently travel with changes in composition, structure, or performance across batches.

options.label: Add independent composition and microscopy checks to every batch
options.reveals: Whether each batch's measurements agree across methods, without linking differences back to how the batch was made.

options.label: Re-measure released batches to tighter tolerance
options.reveals: More precise values for material already released, without explaining the process conditions that produced those values.

options.label: Raise production throughput with records unchanged
options.reveals: How much more material can be produced, while preserving the same blind spot about why batches differ.

failure_feedback.consequence: the programme gets better numbers on old material but still cannot connect a future difference to the process that produced it
more batches are produced under the same weak traceability
failure_feedback.line: You scaled the blind spot with the production rate.

dayTitle: Complete the evidence chain—and confront responsibility
title: Scientific responsibility after Trinity
task: Which statement best separates the laboratory's technical responsibility from the political decision that follows?
scene: After Trinity, reports of yield, fallout, and measurement uncertainty are spread across the laboratory. Officials outside the site are asking what the results mean. Scientists now have to decide what belongs in their technical assessment before it leaves Los Alamos.
takeaway: Technical expertise carries a duty to communicate consequences and uncertainty clearly without turning expertise into political authority.
why: Scientists can report what the instruments measured. They can estimate likely effects and state how uncertain those estimates are. That information matters because officials cannot judge consequences they have never been shown. Scientists can also explain which conclusions are well supported and which depend on assumptions. They do not get the final policy decision simply because they know the technical details. Their responsibility is to make the evidence and uncertainty clear before others decide what to do with it.
assumes: a technical question and a decision about its use are different questions
answerText: Provide the technical consequences and uncertainties clearly, and distinguish that assessment from any policy recommendation. Expertise informs the decision without becoming the authority that makes it.

choices: Provide a clear technical account of expected consequences and uncertainties, while labeling separately any policy recommendation.
Limit the laboratory's contribution to raw instrument readings, because translating them into expected consequences would cross into policy.
Treat scientific expertise as authority to decide the policy, because the laboratory understands the technical facts better than outside officials.
Withhold a technical assessment until political leaders choose a course, so the laboratory cannot be seen as influencing the decision.
rebuttals: Raw measurements require technical interpretation before non-specialists can understand their consequences; refusing that interpretation withholds part of the expertise.
Expertise strengthens a technical assessment but does not by itself confer authority over the political decision.
Waiting until after the decision defeats the purpose of technical advice: the relevant consequences and uncertainties are needed before the choice is made.
text.setup: Separate what scientific expertise can establish from who has authority to decide.
